title: Claw — Brain
description: Operational dashboard for the Claw Brain. Every panel carries a description saying what it measures, how to read it, and what is normal versus what should worry you. Thresholds assume the upstream defaults (MAX_CONCURRENT=3, MAX_RESIDENT=6, brain.replicas=3); adjust the panel maxima if your deployment overrides them.

panels.title: Overview — is Claw healthy at a glance
Prompt Cache Hit Ratio
panels.description: Whether the prompt cache is actually working, measured two ways at once. The token series is cache_read / (input + cache_read + cache_create) from claw_brain_llm_tokens_total — the share of prompt tokens that were billed at the cached rate, i.e. the real saving. The turn series is claw_brain_llm_cache_turns_total{state="hit"} over all turns — how often a request read anything back at all; state is derived from what the response reported, where "hit" means cache_read > 0, "write" means only a create, "miss" means the provider spoke and returned nothing, and "unreported"/"off" mean it said nothing about caching, so those turns move the turn ratio without being real misses. Both series sum across all brain pods before dividing; never average per-pod ratios. Read the two together: a high token ratio with a healthy turn ratio is a working cache; a mid-range 0.5–0.85 usually means the cached prefix keeps being broken — tool-list changes, a compaction rewriting history, or cache_control breakpoints drifting position — and is worth investigating against the breakpoints_sent distribution. A ratio collapsing toward zero while requests keep flowing is the failure this panel exists to catch: markers are still being sent and nothing is read back, so every turn is paid at full price; pair it with the cache failure detectors and the breakpoint distribution to find where the prefix diverges. Note that the denominator deliberately includes only the three kinds providers actually report — a missing kind means the provider cannot report it, which is not the same as zero. The third series splits the token ratio by the wire protocol that reported it, which the aggregate cannot show: the two wires differ in what they can observe — an OpenAI-shaped backend may report no cache writes and no TTL breakdown at all — so a fleet speaking both, mid-rollout or after a backend switch, sums measurements together with blind spots. If the aggregate ever sits near 0.50 while the turn ratio stays healthy, suspect token accounting before you suspect the cache: that is the arithmetic signature of the cached portion landing on both sides of the division, not of a cache missing half the time.

panels.title: Execution slots in use (fleet)
panels.description: How many tasks across the whole fleet currently hold an execution slot, summing claw_brain_gate_inflight ("Tasks holding an execution slot on this pod") over every brain pod. This is an instantaneous water level, not a rate. The ceiling is MAX_CONCURRENT per pod times the replica count — with upstream defaults MAX_CONCURRENT=3 and brain.replicas=3 that is 9 fleet-wide, so rescale this panel's max if you changed either. Comfortable is anything up to roughly 70% of that ceiling; sitting near it means the fleet is close to saturated and new deliveries can only queue or be refused. Pegged at the ceiling with a non-zero queue behind it is a capacity problem: add replicas or raise MAX_CONCURRENT, since the NATS prefetch window is not what admits work — the execution gate is.

panels.title: Queued deliveries (fleet)
panels.description: Deliveries fleet-wide that have been taken by a pod and are waiting for an execution slot, summing claw_brain_gate_queued ("Deliveries on this pod waiting for an execution slot"). It is the overflow behind inflight: the gate holds the delivery loop rather than parking a task that already owns a distributed lock, so a backlog shows up here instead of as a redelivery storm. There is no hard bound on it: a delivery past its refusal allowance is kept rather than handed back, so the queue can grow above the nominal residency ceiling. What bounds it in practice is per-pod queue depth — the MAX_RESIDENT + MAX_CONCURRENT residency ceiling less the runs already resident, i.e. MAX_CONCURRENT of headroom with the upstream defaults. The gauge maximum is fleet-wide queue depth, MAX_CONCURRENT × brain.replicas = 9 with the upstream defaults; rescale if you changed either. Healthy is a flat zero with occasional few-second spikes as work lands. A queue that stays above zero means pods are at their cap and the backlog is not draining. A delivery arriving at a pod whose execution gate will not admit it (inflight at MAX_CONCURRENT, or inflight+parked at MAX_RESIDENT) is refused as delivery_refused{reason="surplus"} and nak'd back to NATS, spending one of the TASK_MAX_DELIVER budget of that message — but only SURPLUS_REFUSALS times; past that the pod keeps it and it lands here. At that point the fix is more replicas, not more prefetch.

panels.title: Parked runs (fleet)
panels.description: Runs fleet-wide in the parked state, summing claw_brain_gate_parked ("Runs on this pod waiting on something external, holding a sandbox and no slot") — runs blocked on a user approving a tool call, or on a long background command. Parking hands the execution slot back but not the sandbox, so a parked run costs no concurrency and still costs memory and a residency place; the ceiling is MAX_RESIDENT per pod (6 by default, i.e. 18 across three replicas — adjust if you changed MAX_RESIDENT or the replica count). A handful, drifting with how much human approval is in the loop, is normal. Inflight near zero while this number is large means the fleet is not idle, it is waiting on people. Parked approaching the residency ceiling is a harder block than a queue: the pod has no room to admit anything new, and resuming a parked run outranks admitting a fresh delivery, so the backlog behind it stops moving until the humans come back.

panels.title: Held deliveries (fleet)
panels.description: Deliveries the fleet has taken responsibility for and not yet settled, summing claw_brain_deliveries_held. It covers all three states at once — queued, executing and parked — and is deliberately counted even above the ceiling, because releasing the count early would make a pod look empty while the overflow is still held and let surplus be admitted on top of it. The per-pod ceiling is MAX_RESIDENT + MAX_CONCURRENT (9 with the upstream defaults; 27 across three replicas). Normally it tracks inflight + queued + parked closely. The shape to worry about is held climbing steadily while inflight is stuck at its cap and nothing completes: deliveries are being caught but not run, which is exactly the stall a liveness endpoint cannot see. Check the execution gate for a slot leak — an acquire with no matching release — before assuming it is load.

panels.title: Watchdog Worst Pod (now)
panels.description: The current worst value of claw_brain_watchdog_last_tick_age_seconds across all brain pods: seconds since that pod's own setInterval(1s) watchdog tick last fired. It is deliberately max() rather than avg(), because an average over healthy replicas hides the one pod that has stopped ticking, and the watchdog is deliberately decoupled from any session keepalive so a single busy session cannot make a hung pod look alive. Read it as a worst-case summary of the fleet: green means every pod is still ticking; anything else sends you to the per-pod series to find which one. Healthy oscillates 0–2s. Above 10s means real event-loop lag on some pod. Above 60s means that pod is hung, and its INV-13 session lock is at imminent risk of expiring while it still believes it holds it — which is how two pods end up running the same session.

panels.title: Poison Unresolved (24h)
panels.description: How often the poison guard gave up entirely, from claw_brain_task_poison_unresolved_total over the last 24 hours. The guard fires one delivery before NATS would drop the task and tries to close it out cleanly; this counter increments when the terminal handoff — emitting the completion event, delivering agent-done, acking — kept failing right through the final delivery, so the message was terminated while the session row is still marked running. It is the residual silent drop the guard cannot fix, because what is broken is the resolution path itself. Read the number as a count of sessions currently stuck in running that need closing by hand, not as a rate. Steady state must be zero, and a flat zero line or No data is the healthy picture. Any increment at all is worth chasing immediately, and the thing to chase is the completion path — event emission, the outbox, the backend task callback — rather than the task; the by-reason breakdown says which class of task was affected, and the corresponding sessions have to be moved to a terminal state manually.

panels.title: Lossy redeliveries (no checkpoint), 24h
panels.description: Redeliveries that found nothing to resume from: claw_brain_checkpoint_resume_total{result="miss_redelivery"} over 24 hours — a run that had been delivered before, so a previous attempt existed, yet no usable v3 checkpoint was in KV. The whole run restarts from turn zero and everything the earlier attempt did is repeated. Treat it as an incident count, not a water level; any non-zero value is worth opening the timeline above to see which release or which pod it landed on. Zero is the expected value. One or more means the checkpoint write that should have preceded that redelivery failed, or the checkpoint expired before the redelivery arrived; check claw_brain_checkpoint_writes_total{result="failure"} and the SIGTERM checkpoint path. Several a day means the graceful-shutdown window is too short for the work in flight — with terminationGracePeriodSeconds at the chart default of 300s, checkpoints are not landing before the pod goes away, and either the writes are slow or the sync ahead of them is. Note the sibling counter claw_brain_task_redelivery_total{has_checkpoint="false"} is not this number: it also ticks for every first delivery, which legitimately has no checkpoint.

panels.title: Workspace Sync Failure Ratio (30m)
panels.description: The share of syncWorkspace() attempts across the fleet that threw, over a 30-minute window. The numerator is claw_brain_workspace_sync_failures_total; the denominator adds that to claw_brain_workspace_sync_duration_seconds_count, which is only observed on the success path, so the two together are the full attempt count — the clamp_min and the or vector(0) exist so an idle window returns 0 rather than NaN. A failed sync means that round of .claw/workspaces/<sid>/current/ never landed on the shared filesystem, so whatever the session resumes from after a SIGTERM or a rolling restart is the previous snapshot, and the work since then is gone. Steady state should be 0; occasional blips under a couple of percent are single-sandbox noise. A sustained few percent calls for the failure-reason breakdown below (timeout, hands_unreachable, meta_write_error, config_error, empty_workspace, rsync_error). A single config_error is the one to act on immediately — that pod's persistence root is not mounted and every sync it attempts is a no-op. Anything approaching ten percent means the shared filesystem or the Hands channel is broadly unhealthy — at that point any rolling restart will lose workspaces at scale, so fix the sync before restarting anything. Note the sync paths have their own concurrency limits (WORKSPACE_SYNC_NORMAL_SLOTS and WORKSPACE_SIGTERM_PRIORITY_SLOTS, both 4 by default), so timeouts here can also mean queueing behind those slots. No data does not mean healthy — it means no sync ran in the window at all, which is itself worth explaining.

panels.title: Cache Failure Detectors (must stay at zero)
panels.description: Three counters that are supposed to be permanently flat at zero, drawn together because they are three early symptoms of one thing: the cache quietly ceasing to work. claw_brain_prompt_size_unknown_total counts turns where no provider reported a prompt size; auto-compaction is the only context-length guard in the loop and it needs a number to compare against COMPACTION_TRIGGER_INPUT_TOKENS (850000 by default), so a run flying blind looks exactly like a healthy run right up to the moment the context window rejects a request outright. claw_brain_llm_cache_entry_lost_total counts turns that sent markers, had already written cache earlier -- in this process or in an earlier delivery of the same run -- and read nothing back — behaviour-based, so it works on transports that report no TTL breakdown at all, though it still requires the response to have explicitly reported cache_read, since a turn whose usage never arrived must not be blamed on the cache; its gap label separates over_ttl, consistent with an entry that lived shorter than the TTL this deployment configured, from under_ttl, which points at the prefix rather than the lifetime. The threshold follows LLM_CACHE_TTL, not a fixed five minutes. claw_brain_llm_cache_disabled_total counts sessions that stopped sending cache_control after the gateway rejected the markers, meaning the rest of that session runs uncached at full price. Read them as booleans, not magnitudes: any line leaving the zero axis is the alert, and the height only tells you how fast. Healthy is all three pinned at zero; a sustained non-zero rate on any of them outranks everything else on this row, and the cache_entry_lost gap breakdown is the first place to go to decide between a TTL problem and a prefix problem.

panels.title: Task duration distribution
panels.description: How run durations are distributed over time, the panel to reach for once a quantile has moved and you need to know whether the whole population shifted or split in two. A single warm band drifting upward is every run getting slower — model or tool latency, or a saturated execution gate making runs wait behind siblings on the same pod. Two bands is two populations, which is the ordinary picture when short interactive turns share a fleet with long agent runs and is not by itself a problem. The failure this exposes that the quantiles hide is a new band appearing at the bottom, against the 1s and 5s edges: short runs are only cheap when they were meant to be short, so a mass of sub-5s runs appearing alongside a rising redelivery share is pickups aborting on arrival rather than fast work. The top edge is 1800s and everything longer collects in the overflow row, which is the one part of this panel you cannot size by eye — a growing overflow row means runs are outliving the histogram. Bucket boundaries are fixed in the metric declaration at [1,5,15,30,60,120,300,600,1800]; the visible resolution is those edges and no finer, so do not read structure inside a band.

panels.title: Task terminal success ratio
panels.description: The share of runs that ended for good and ended well: ok over ok plus failed, across the dashboard's time range. retryable and interrupted are excluded from both halves deliberately — a retryable run has not resolved anything yet, it is on its way back to the queue and will report again, and an interrupted run is a user's decision; including either would turn this into a measure of queue churn or of how often people change their mind rather than of whether the system can finish the work it is given. The denominator is intentionally left unguarded, so a range in which nothing terminated reads No data instead of a fake red 0%. Healthy deployments sit at or very near 1, because a failed run is a fatal error, a run that hit its deadline, or a sandbox the provider would not build — none of which resolve themselves. Anything sustained below roughly 0.98 should be read next to the outcome-rate panel to see which branch produces it. A high ratio here is also not sufficient on its own: if it stays near 1 while the redelivery share climbs, tasks are finishing only after being handed back repeatedly.

panels.title: Sandbox cold-start success ratio
panels.description: The share of sandbox creation attempts that produced a working sandbox, over the dashboard's range. Only a call that actually built one is counted: reuse of a healthy cached sandbox and the local-dev short-circuit both return without creating anything and are not creation attempts, so this is the success rate of the slow path alone, not of sandbox acquisition in general. A throw is counted as a failed attempt even when it came out of the reuse probe that runs first, because by then the caller has no sandbox either way, and counting only the failures that happen after the decision to create would hide exactly the provisioning outages this metric exists to show. The denominator is left unguarded so that a range with no cold starts reads No data rather than a red 0% — a deployment serving warm sessions can legitimately create nothing for long stretches, and that is not a failure. Expect this at or near 1. Errors here are the control plane refusing or failing to schedule the workload, an image that will not pull, or a sandbox that never answered /health, and each one reaches a user as a session that cannot start. Sustained below roughly 0.97 should be read together with the create/destroy rate panel, since a provisioning problem that also drives attempts up has become a retry storm.

panels.title: Task outcome rate
panels.description: Terminal states of Brain task runs, as seen by the pod that consumed the delivery. run() sets exactly one outcome in each of its terminal branches and reports it once from the finally, so a sample here is a run that ended, not a task that completed — one task can produce several samples across redeliveries. The four values answer different questions and must not be read as four grades of failure: ok is a run whose engine finished and whose agent-done handoff landed; failed is terminal and will not come back (a fatal error, the run budget exhausted at its deadline, a run row already terminal, or a terminal sandbox-provisioning verdict); retryable is everything that gets redelivered — a retryable error, a checkpoint taken on SIGTERM, a lease lost to a second replica that already holds the lock, or a finished run whose agent-done handoff ran out of attempts — meaning the work did not finish on this pod and returns to the queue; interrupted is a user cancelling a run that was working, kept out of failed on purpose so that a failure rate does not end up measuring how often people change their mind. In steady state ok carries the stack and retryable is a thin line that spikes at deploys and drains and then settles. Sustained retryable outside a rollout means runs are repeatedly being taken away from pods, and each occurrence spends one delivery of the task's budget, so enough of them ends with the poison guard resolving the task instead of running it. Any sustained failed line wants a root cause; interrupted is user behaviour and needs none. The rate this can reach is nine concurrent runs divided by typical run duration — with the upstream defaults MAX_CONCURRENT=3 per pod and three brain replicas — so scale your expectation by both if you raised either.

panels.title: Redelivered and interrupted share
panels.description: The two outcomes that are neither success nor defect, each as a share of all runs that ended in the interval. retryable/total is the redelivery rate — how much of the work the fleet performs is work it has already started once, which is the combined cost of drains, lost leases, retryable provider errors and exhausted agent-done handoffs. interrupted/total is how often users stop healthy runs, plotted separately precisely so it can never inflate a failure number. Both denominators use increase() over the same interval clamped to a minimum of 1, so a window with no runs reads zero rather than dividing by nothing. Near-zero redelivery between rollouts is the normal picture, and a rolling update legitimately raises it for the length of the drain: a SIGTERM checkpoint has to complete inside the pod's grace period, which upstream defaults to terminationGracePeriodSeconds=300, so the bump should decay within about five minutes of the last pod going down. A redelivery share that stays in the tens of percent means the same tasks are looping, and since every redelivery consumes one delivery of TASK_MAX_DELIVER, a task that runs the budget out is resolved by the poison guard rather than executed. Interrupt share has no correct value; watch it for changes in shape rather than against a threshold.

panels.title: Task duration quantiles
panels.description: Wall-clock time of a task run, from the moment run() takes the delivery to the moment it reports its outcome, over all four outcomes together. The measurement includes the resume-checkpoint read and any sandbox provisioning the run had to do before its first turn, so it is the latency a user actually experiences and not just model time. p50 says what a typical run costs; the distance between p50 and p99 says where the cost lives — a p99 lifting while p50 stays flat is a handful of runs waiting on sandbox creation or queued behind siblings on the workspace gate, whereas both rising together is the agent work itself getting longer. The histogram's top edge is 1800s, and Prometheus reports a quantile that falls in the overflow bucket as that top edge, so a line pinned exactly at 1800 means "at least half an hour", not "thirty minutes". Duration on its own is not a fault signal, since long agent runs are legitimate; read it against the outcome panels. A rising p50 alongside a rising redelivery share is runs being cut short and repeated, while a quantile pinned at the ceiling alongside rising failed is runs reaching their deadline and being ended by the run budget.

panels.title: Task duration p95 by outcome
panels.description: The same run-duration histogram split by how the run ended, which is where the shape of a problem becomes legible. The ok line is what a completed run costs and is the only one whose absolute value means something on its own. retryable is the whole run's wall clock up to the point it was taken away, not the time spent handing it back, so a drain-driven redelivery reports however long that run had already been going — expect it to sit near the ok line during a rollout. A retryable p95 of seconds is the diagnostic shape: runs dying almost immediately after pickup, a lease lost to another replica, or a provider error on the way to a sandbox. A failed p95 near the top of the range is the run budget expiring at its deadline rather than anything erroring, whereas failed at a few seconds is work rejected before it ever ran, typically a sandbox the provider refused. interrupted simply reports how long users waited before cancelling; a falling interrupted p95 usually means people are giving up sooner, which is a product signal rather than an infrastructure one. Compare the lines' positions relative to each other; the quantiles all pin at 1800s once the true value passes the top bucket.

panels.title: Sandbox cold-start latency
panels.description: How long it takes to build a sandbox and get it answering /health, split by outcome. Reuse is excluded from this histogram entirely, so it is the cost of the slow path and never an average acquisition time — a fleet with good reuse can show a high p95 here and still feel fast to its users, and the way to judge that is the create rate next to it, not this number alone. Use the health gate to place the value: with the upstream defaults HANDS_HEALTH_MAX_TRIES=40 and HANDS_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS=3000, polling alone permits about 120s of the wait, so a p95 under that is mostly Hands starting inside a sandbox that already exists, while a p95 above it is time spent before the container ran at all — image pull, node scheduling, or queueing in the control plane — which is where to look first. Recompute that reference point if you changed either env var. The error line measures something different, the time to give up: errors landing near where ok sits means creations are timing out at the health gate, while errors returning in seconds means the provider is rejecting the request outright, and the two want different fixes. Buckets stop at 600s, so either line pins there once the real value passes it.

panels.title: Cold-start duration distribution
panels.description: Bucket-level distribution of successful sandbox creations, restricted to outcome="ok" so that the timeout mass of failed attempts does not swamp the shape. This shows what the quantiles cannot: whether the slow path is uniformly slow or bimodal. One tight band means provisioning is predictable and its position is simply what your image and node pool cost. Two bands almost always separate sandboxes that landed on a node with the image already cached from those that had to pull it, and the upper band's height is the pull cost you would remove by pre-pulling. A band drifting past the 120s edge is the more serious pattern, because the health poll accounts for at most about 120s under the upstream defaults (HANDS_HEALTH_MAX_TRIES=40 at HANDS_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS=3000) — beyond that the time is scheduling or admission, and creations are then close to the point where they fail rather than merely being slow. Bucket edges are fixed in the metric declaration at [1,5,10,30,60,120,300,600] and everything longer lands in the overflow row; any weight in that row is a sandbox that took over ten minutes to become usable, which most callers will have abandoned.

panels.title: Sandbox create and destroy rate
panels.description: Sandbox lifecycle throughput: creations that succeeded or threw, and teardowns that succeeded or threw, all on one axis so the two halves can be compared directly. Creations count only calls that actually built a sandbox, so this line is cold starts and not sandbox usage. Over a long enough window destroys should track creates, since every sandbox that gets built is eventually stopped at session end, by recovery, or by the reaper; a persistent create surplus is sandboxes accumulating in the cluster, and a persistent destroy surplus is teardown running over sandboxes that reuse would otherwise have kept warm, which pushes work back onto the create line and shows up as latency in the cold-start panels. Creates legitimately rise with new sessions and after a drain, because a session resuming on another pod often finds no cached sandbox waiting for it. What should worry you is either error line lifting off zero: create errors are users who cannot start, and stop errors are worse than their count suggests — the stop error ratio panel explains why. One caveat when reading the stop lines: a provider that exposes no stop endpoint returns without erroring and is counted ok, so stop ok means "nothing refused the teardown", which is not always the same as "the workload is gone".

panels.title: Sandbox stop error ratio
panels.description: The share of teardown attempts that could not be confirmed. destroyHands retries the provider stop three times about a second apart before counting an error, so an increment is not a transient blip but a control plane that would not stop that workload across several seconds. The count matters more than its size because of what happens next: destroyHands rethrows, and every caller of it is on its way to building a replacement sandbox, so the throw stops that replacement — a workload that may still be running must never be orphaned underneath a new one holding the same session's workspace. Each increment is therefore two problems at once, a session that did not get the sandbox it needed and a workload that may still be alive, consuming cluster resources with nothing tracking it. The denominator is clamped to a minimum of 1 so idle windows read zero rather than dividing by nothing. Zero is the only good value: an isolated point is a control plane briefly unhappy, but anything sustained means teardown is broken for a class of sandbox and the orphan set grows for as long as it lasts, so pair it with the create/destroy rate panel to see the accumulating gap, and expect user-visible failures on any session whose sandbox needed replacing. Not visible here: providers with no stop endpoint at all, which return successfully and leave the workload to control-plane garbage collection.

panels.title: Execution slot saturation over time
panels.description: Four gauges share one axis because they are four water marks of the same story across the fleet, each summed over the brain pods: inflight is tasks holding an execution slot, queued is deliveries waiting for one, parked is runs that handed their slot back but still hold a sandbox while they wait on something external (an approval, a background command), and held is every delivery a pod has taken responsibility for and not yet settled — roughly the sum of the other three, since it counts queued, executing and parked deliveries alike. Read the levels against the ceilings the gate enforces: per pod inflight cannot exceed MAX_CONCURRENT, inflight+parked cannot exceed MAX_RESIDENT, and held is bounded by MAX_RESIDENT+MAX_CONCURRENT — with the upstream defaults (MAX_CONCURRENT=3, MAX_RESIDENT=6, ceiling 9) and the chart's brain.replicas=3 that is 9, 18 and 27 fleet-wide, which is the scale these fleet-summed lines are read against; recompute any dashed ceiling lines if you changed either env var or the replica count. The healthy shape is inflight oscillating, queued near zero, parked low, and held tracking the sum. Three shapes deserve attention: queued lifting and staying lifted means every replica is full and the fix is more replicas; inflight sinking while parked and held stay high means runs are stuck waiting on something external, or slots are not being released; and a persistent gap between held and inflight+queued+parked means the counters disagree — look at the gate release path, because a slot or a residency place kept for a delivery that no longer exists permanently shrinks what that pod will ever accept.

panels.title: Slots per pod vs MAX_CONCURRENT
panels.description: The one panel in this row deliberately split by pod: execution slots occupied on each brain replica, capped per pod by MAX_CONCURRENT (upstream default 3 — raise the reference line if you changed it). What matters here is balance across the series, not the total: the task consumer is pull-based, so replicas should draw work at roughly the same rate and their curves should interleave inside one band. Worry when one pod sits pinned at the cap while others sit near zero — that pod is holding long-running tasks or has leaked slots, and it will start refusing deliveries with reason="surplus" even though the fleet total still looks like it has room. A curve that vanishes and restarts at zero is a pod restart; restarts push their unsettled deliveries back to the stream, so read the redelivery panels below alongside it.

panels.title: Delivery residency utilisation per pod (ceiling 9)
panels.description: Held deliveries on each pod as a fraction of its residency ceiling, MAX_RESIDENT+MAX_CONCURRENT (9 with the upstream defaults) — in other words how much more work that replica can take on. The ceiling sits deliberately above the gate's resident cap: it counts deliveries queued, executing and parked, while the gate counts only runs, and the extra MAX_CONCURRENT is the queue depth that keeps a pod from going idle between finishing one run and being offered the next. Fuller bar, less headroom. A pod refuses new deliveries on its execution gate, not on this bar: delivery_refused{reason="surplus"} fires when inflight is at MAX_CONCURRENT or inflight+parked is at MAX_RESIDENT, which happens well before this bar fills. A full bar means the pod is also holding deliveries it has run out of refusals for. Below 0.7 is comfortable, 0.7–0.9 means the pod is working out of its queue rather than off the stream, and at or above 0.9 it is effectively only draining. One bar high while the rest are low points at that replica; most bars high at once is fleet capacity, not a sick pod.

panels.title: Task redeliveries by checkpoint
panels.description: claw_brain_task_redelivery_total is incremented once per run when the runner classifies its resume state, labelled has_checkpoint="true" when a usable checkpoint was read back from the KV store and "false" when the run had to start from nothing; this graph shows the 5-minute increase of each. Read the two lines as a ratio rather than as absolute counts: "true" is work that survives an interruption — the run picks up from the checkpoint and loses only the progress since the last write — while "false" is work with nothing to resume from, so any redelivery of it repeats the whole task. Because the counter also ticks for first deliveries, which legitimately have no checkpoint, a steady "false" baseline proportional to new task volume is expected; what matters is "false" rising when tasks are being redelivered rather than newly started. Small clusters on both lines during a rolling restart are normal, since draining pods hand their deliveries back. Sustained "false" growth without matching new-task volume means checkpoints are not being written, or are written too late to be read back — check claw_brain_checkpoint_writes_total{kind="sigterm"} for failures and claw_brain_checkpoint_resume_total{result="miss_redelivery"}, which is the delivery-count-aware version of the same question. Both lines climbing together means pods are being evicted often or deliveries are timing out before they are acked.

panels.title: Redelivery breakdown (24h)
panels.description: The same counter as the graph above, totalled over 24 hours and read as a two-row roster: has_checkpoint is a closed set of "true" and "false" in the source, so these two rows are the whole population. The number to look at is the split, not either total — it says what share of runs the pod could have resumed from a checkpoint if something had interrupted them. A row count that tracks your task volume with "true" dominating for long-lived sessions is the ordinary picture; a "false" share that climbs day over day means runs are increasingly starting from scratch, and the checkpoint write path is where to look. Because the counter also increments on first deliveries, compare the split to the previous day rather than to zero.

panels.title: Deliveries refused by reason
panels.description: The rate at which this pod hands a delivery back without running it, split by the closed label set the refusal path emits: "surplus" means the execution gate would not admit the run — inflight is at MAX_CONCURRENT, or inflight+parked is at MAX_RESIDENT — so the message is nak'd for another replica, and "drain" means the pod is shutting down or has been marked drained and is no longer taking work. Neither is an error, but both spend one of the message's finite deliveries, which is why the refusal path only allows a delivery to be refused a bounded number of times and never within one delivery of the poison guard's threshold: a refusal must never be the redelivery that gets a healthy task written off as poisoned. Expect "drain" as short spikes confined to deployment windows and "surplus" flat at zero. Sustained "surplus" is fleet capacity, and the queued and held lines above will confirm it; "drain" outside a deployment means pods are being evicted or restarted repeatedly. An empty panel simply means no delivery has ever been refused.

panels.title: Surplus refusals per pod (1h)
panels.description: Deliveries each pod handed back in the last hour because its own execution gate was full (reason="surplus"). Read it as a ranking that answers one question: is the fleet out of capacity, or is one replica stuck? All zero is the expected state. One or two pods carrying the whole count usually means long-running tasks or slots that were never released on those replicas — cross-check them against the per-pod slots panel, where they will be pinned at MAX_CONCURRENT. Every pod showing a number at once is genuine fleet saturation and calls for more replicas rather than an investigation of any single pod.

panels.title: Checkpoint write failure ratio
panels.description: Share of NATS KV checkpoint writes that failed over the last hour, summed across every brain replica (the chart ships brain.replicas=3). Read it as a current-health number, not a trend: the denominator is all writes in the same window, so in a quiet hour a single failure pushes the ratio far up — pair it with the writes-by-kind/result rate panel to see the absolute count behind the percentage. Steady state must be exactly zero, and this is not a metric with an acceptable error budget. A rejected write does not retry and does not stop the run: the run keeps executing while permanently losing its ability to resume, and the only outward signal is one sandboxStatus=checkpoint_write_failed event carrying payload_bytes. Anything above zero is worth chasing; anything sustained above 1% has a systemic cause, normally payloads over the bucket's max_value_size (BRAIN_CHECKPOINTS_MAX_VALUE_BYTES, 16 MiB by default) or a checkpoints bucket that is not writable at all.

panels.title: Checkpoint payload p95 vs 16 MB bucket ceiling
panels.description: p95 of claw_brain_checkpoint_payload_bytes — the serialized checkpoint at the moment it is put into NATS KV. The payload carries the session's entire messages array, so it grows monotonically with conversation length rather than fluctuating with load. Read it as a water level against a fixed ceiling: the gauge maximum is the top histogram bucket edge, 16,000,000 bytes, which sits just under the bucket's default max_value_size of 16 MiB; a full gauge means writes are about to be rejected. Long sessions normally land somewhere between a few hundred KB and about 1 MB. Past roughly 5 MB something is accumulating context without bound — check that auto-compaction is firing (COMPACTION_TRIGGER_INPUT_TOKENS defaults to 850000 input tokens); past roughly 12 MB it must be dealt with before it actually crosses the ceiling, because once a put is rejected that run becomes silently unresumable while continuing to run normally. Both the gauge max and those thresholds assume the default BRAIN_CHECKPOINTS_MAX_VALUE_BYTES=16 MiB; scale them if your deployment sets the bucket larger or smaller.

panels.title: Redelivery checkpoint hit rate
panels.description: Of the resumes over the last 6 hours that were actually redeliveries, the fraction that found a usable checkpoint in KV: hit / (hit + miss_redelivery). miss_first_delivery is deliberately excluded from the denominator — a brand-new task having no checkpoint is the expected case, and counting it would dilute the only signal here. Read it as a single current-health number answering one question: when a task genuinely needed to be recovered, was its state there. The target is 100%; below 99% deserves attention and below 95% is an incident, because every miss is a task that was re-dispatched and lost all prior progress, which the user sees as work starting over. Two lines of enquiry when it drops: claw_brain_checkpoint_writes_total{result="failure"} (the state was never written), and the checkpoint TTL versus the redelivery window (it was written but expired first) — CHECKPOINT_TTL_MS defaults to 24h against a consumer ack_wait that defaults to 2 minutes, so an expiry-driven miss means the TTL has been shortened well below its default.

panels.title: SLO-1a / SLO-1b resume quality
panels.description: Two resume-quality ratios derived from claw_brain_resume_workspace_mode_total, which metrics.ts declares as the source SLO-1a and SLO-1b are computed from. SLO-1a is workspace recovery success — (sandbox_reuse + workspace_restore) over those two plus no_data_turn0, i.e. of the runs that genuinely had to be recovered, how many got their working directory back. SLO-1b is the hot-path share — sandbox_reuse over the same denominator, i.e. how many resumed with no sandbox rebuild and no rsync at all. Both denominators exclude skip_no_ckpt, since a task with no checkpoint was never a resume. Read them together: 1a says whether the user's files survived, 1b says how cheaply. High 1a with low 1b is an acceptable degradation — the sandbox was rebuilt but the workspace was pulled back, just slowly; low 1a is data loss regardless of 1b. Expect 1a above 99%, and treat below 95% as user-visible loss traceable to SIGTERM workspace sync timeouts and errors. 1b has no hard target but should dominate during ordinary rolling restarts, because redelivery normally lands inside the 2-minute default ack_wait while SANDBOX_IDLE_REUSE_MS keeps the sandbox for 15 minutes; 1b falling off means sandbox lifetime no longer covers the redelivery window. One deployment caveat: WORKSPACE_PERSIST_BASE is empty by default, which disables shared-filesystem persistence entirely — SIGTERM then falls back to an S3 sync and resume falls through to the S3 baseline restore, which is still recorded as no_data_turn0. On such a deployment SLO-1a reads low by construction and only sandbox_reuse lifts it, so configure WORKSPACE_PERSIST_BASE before reading 1a as a loss signal.

panels.title: Checkpoint writes by kind / result
panels.description: Rate of writes into the checkpoints KV bucket, split by the code path that issued them and by outcome. kind="turn" is the routine write at the end of each agent turn, kind="sigterm" is the last-chance write from the SIGTERM catch block, and kind="post_sync" is the re-write that flips has_workspace_sync=true after a workspace sync completes; result is success or failure. This is the mechanism that lets a half-finished run survive a pod restart at all. Read the lines as 5-minute rates: turn/success should carry the bulk and rise and fall with concurrent runs, while sigterm/success should be zero except during rollouts or evictions. Note that the post_sync series is currently always empty — the post-sync re-write does not pass its kind argument and so defaults to "turn"; that is a code defect, not a scrape problem, and post_sync volume is hidden inside the turn line. Any failure series leaving zero needs immediate attention: the consequence is not a retry but a run that continues executing with no way back, since a payload above the bucket's max_value_size is rejected outright. When failures appear, cross-check the payload-size panels to tell an oversized payload apart from NATS instability. Sigterm writes outside a planned rollout mean pods are being evicted unexpectedly.

panels.title: Checkpoint payload size distribution
panels.description: The full distribution of serialized checkpoint sizes over time, rather than a single quantile. The histogram buckets are 10K, 50K, 200K, 1M, 5M and 16M bytes, and the last edge, 16,000,000 bytes, sits just under the bucket's default max_value_size of 16 MiB (BRAIN_CHECKPOINTS_MAX_VALUE_BYTES). Time runs along the x axis, payload size up the y axis, and colour intensity is how many writes landed in that band — what matters is the shape of the band and which way it is drifting, not any single cell. A healthy picture is most of the heat sitting in a stable band roughly between 50K and 1M. Slow upward drift is context accumulating in long sessions: tolerable, but worth watching. Samples appearing in the top 5M–16M band are the warning: those sessions are approaching the value limit and the next write may be rejected, taking the run's resumability with it. Persistent heat in the top band means some sessions' message history is never being trimmed — check that auto-compaction is running for them (COMPACTION_TRIGGER_INPUT_TOKENS defaults to 850000).

panels.title: KV write latency p50 / p95 by kind
panels.description: End-to-end duration of a single checkpoint put into NATS KV, split by write kind. Serialization is deliberately excluded — JSON.stringify time is measured separately by claw_brain_checkpoint_serialize_duration_seconds — so this reflects NATS-side write performance only; the histogram tops out at 5s. Read p95 against p50 per kind: the two separating means a tail, usually large payloads or queueing on the NATS side rather than a uniform slowdown. Expect p95 in the tens of milliseconds, which is what the dense 0.005–0.05 bucket region is sized for. p95 above 0.25s says KV is queueing or payloads have grown heavy; above 1s deserves real concern, because the SIGTERM checkpoint is the final step inside the pod's termination grace window (terminationGracePeriodSeconds=300 in the chart) and a slow KV eats margin that is already committed elsewhere. The kind="sigterm" series in particular should stay short.

panels.title: SIGTERM checkpoint duration vs 300s grace
panels.description: Wall-clock time spent inside the whole SIGTERM catch block — draining any in-flight workspace sync, running the priority sync, emitting taskInterrupted, flushing the transcript, and finally writing the KV checkpoint — split by the sync outcome. Read the p95 curves against the 300s line, which is both the chart's default terminationGracePeriodSeconds and the top histogram bucket edge. That line is not a soft target: if the handler has not finished by then kubelet sends SIGKILL, the checkpoint never lands, and that run's progress is gone, so this panel measures directly whether rolling restarts eat user work. The designed budget adds up to about 93s (15s pending-sync drain from SIGTERM_PENDING_SYNC_WAIT_MS, then priority workspace sync, event emission and transcript flush), so a p95 under ~100s is healthy and leaves roughly threefold headroom. Past 180s most of that headroom is gone, typically because workspaces have grown and syncs take longer; approaching 300s means runs are already being SIGKILLed mid-checkpoint, and the fix is either a larger grace period or a smaller workspace sync. Both the line and these thresholds assume the chart default of 300s — move them if your deployment sets a different grace period. Any sync_result="timeout" or "error" series means the workspace did not persist, so those runs can only come back as no_data_turn0.

panels.title: SIGTERM workspace sync outcomes (24h)
panels.description: Count of SIGTERM checkpoints in the last 24 hours grouped by sync_result, taken from the _count of the SIGTERM duration histogram. success means the workspace was persisted before the pod exited; timeout means the sync exceeded its deadline (the error text matched a timeout); error means it failed some other way; skipped means there was nothing worth saving — no completed turn, no hands client, or a fallback upload that found no files. Read it as a small name-and-count list whose composition is the point; the total should land near the number of SIGTERMed pods times the runs resident on each, which is bounded by MAX_RESIDENT (default 6, twice the default MAX_CONCURRENT=3), so a total far below that means runs are not reaching this path at all. success should dominate, with a small amount of skipped from runs that had not finished a turn yet. timeout and error are the rows that matter: they mean the workspace never landed, so the redelivered task can only resume as no_data_turn0 and the user finds an empty working directory after work was done. If either stays non-zero, break it down by reason via claw_brain_workspace_sync_failures_total. Note that with WORKSPACE_PERSIST_BASE unset — the upstream default — the shared-filesystem sync is skipped entirely and these outcomes describe the S3 fallback instead.

panels.title: Resume outcome breakdown (24h)
panels.description: How the checkpoint readback went at the start of each run over the last 24 hours, recorded exactly once per run (the recorder is idempotent). hit means a usable v3 checkpoint was in KV; miss_first_delivery means none was found but this was delivery 1, which is simply how new tasks start; miss_redelivery means none was found even though the task had been delivered before — it was re-dispatched and the previous attempt's progress cannot be located. Read the ranking rather than the absolute numbers, and read miss_redelivery first: splitting the misses into these two values exists precisely to separate the expected turn-0 miss from the one that should never happen. miss_first_delivery is normally the largest bar and is fine; hit volume should track how often redelivery and rolling restarts occur. miss_redelivery should sit at approximately zero — non-zero means work was lost between deliveries, usually a failed write (cross-check writes_total{result="failure"}) or a checkpoint TTL that expired before the redelivery arrived. Three further values are declared on the counter — skip_expired, skip_invalid_version and miss_unexpected — but no code path currently emits them, so they stay empty; if one ever appears, a new readback validation branch has been added and the diff should be read before interpreting the panel.

panels.title: Resume workspace mode over time
panels.description: How the working directory came back on each resume, as 5-minute rates over four modes. sandbox_reuse means the sandbox was still alive (ensureHands returned created=false after its health probe), so /workspace was untouched — fastest and most complete. workspace_restore means the sandbox was rebuilt but the previous checkpoint had has_workspace_sync=true, so the workspace was rsynced back from the shared filesystem. no_data_turn0 means the sandbox was rebuilt with no usable workspace sync, so /workspace starts empty and only the S3 baseline restore is attempted — this turn's output is gone. skip_no_ckpt means there was no checkpoint at all, a new task rather than a resume. During a rolling restart the three non-skip lines all lift at once; which of them lifts is the reading, since their order is exactly resume quality from best to worst. In steady state skip_no_ckpt should dominate. Inside a restart window sandbox_reuse should lead, because redelivery normally arrives within the 2-minute default ack_wait while SANDBOX_IDLE_REUSE_MS keeps an idle sandbox for 15 minutes. workspace_restore rising means sandboxes are being rebuilt — acceptable but slow. no_data_turn0 rising is the one to act on: it is the path where users actually lose their working directory, and it points back at the SIGTERM workspace sync, so check the timeout and error rows of the SIGTERM outcomes table. Note that no_data_turn0 is also what a deployment with WORKSPACE_PERSIST_BASE unset records by default, since workspace_restore requires shared-filesystem persistence to be configured.

panels.title: Resume notice filter activity (NP1-2)
panels.description: Counts passes of the agent loop's resume-notice filter that actually dropped at least one "[system-notice]:" message. Every resume that lost workspace or checkpoint state injects such a notice into the conversation, and those messages stay in the checkpoint's message array forever, so a session that survives several rolling restarts accumulates copies — roughly 50 tokens each, billed on every subsequent request, and enough repetition that the model may read it as being stuck in a degraded loop. The filter keeps only the most recent three (RESUME_NOTICE_KEEP_RECENT=3) and never rewrites the persisted messages, so KV stays a monotonic audit trail. Read the hourly increase as accumulated prompt-pollution pressure rather than as an event count: the filter runs on every LLM attempt, so one long-lived session holding four or more notices keeps this line permanently non-zero. This is also the signal the NP1-2 chaos-test row watches. Steady state should be near zero, since most sessions never see four degraded resumes; a small burst after a rolling restart is expected. A sustained high value means some sessions are repeatedly taking the degraded resume path — check whether no_data_turn0 is climbing at the same time, which would say the same sessions keep losing their workspace.

panels.title: INV-13 Lock Release Skipped (24h)
panels.description: Counts how often releaseSessionLock found that the NATS KV session lock it was about to delete no longer belongs to this pod, and therefore refused to delete it. INV-13 is the invariant that a session lock may only be removed by its rightful holder: if a pod's event loop stalls past the lock bucket's TTL, another pod legitimately acquires the lock, and a blind delete from the stalled pod would open an unlocked window in which two brain replicas run the same session at once. Every increment is one time that protection fired and prevented exactly that. Read it as the 24h increase summed over all brain replicas — a bigger number means holder identity is being contested more often, not that anything was corrupted. Steady state must be 0. Any non-zero value is worth investigating and usually means one of two things: several brain replicas racing for the same session, or a holder mismatch after a pause/resume. A sustained count in the high single digits or above points at a pod stalling for long periods; cross-check claw_brain_watchdog_last_tick_age_seconds, where anything above 60s means the pod is hung and its locks are about to expire underneath it.

panels.title: Poison Deferred: already_running_final (24h)
panels.description: Counts the deliveries where the poison guard, on the very last delivery a message will ever get, recognised that the message is currently being executed by a handler in this cluster (the lock records the stream sequence it was taken for, and it equals this message's seq) and so deliberately left the message unsettled — neither nak nor term. This outcome gets its own tile because it is the one ending that is correct by design yet still a blind spot: the running handler owns the ack, so not touching the message is right, but if that handler dies the task dies with it and nothing surfaces it until the ack_wait window lapses. Read it as the 24h increase across all replicas — it is not an error rate, it is how many times a task was still running after burning its entire redelivery budget down to the last slot. Occasional single digits are normal for genuinely long tasks. A sustained double-digit count means the redelivery budget is short relative to task duration, or something is holding a lock indefinitely; correlate with sessions that never produced an exec_complete, and consider raising TASK_MAX_DELIVER (default 23, with the guard firing one delivery earlier at 22) or narrowing lock granularity so siblings do not queue on one key.

panels.title: Poison Guard Discards by reason
panels.description: The rate at which the brain's own poison guard actually fires — declaring a task dead and closing it out with a user-visible exec_complete(failed) — rather than letting NATS silently drop the message once its redelivery budget runs out. The guard is wired to trigger at TASK_POISON_DELIVERY_COUNT = TASK_MAX_DELIVER - 1, i.e. the last delivery before the stream would have discarded the message with the session still marked running. Read it as three per-second lines summed over all brain replicas, one per reason, and treat the reasons as separate problems: max_retries_exceeded means the task really does keep failing and needs a root cause; lock_contention_exhausted means the task itself is healthy and was killed by a queue — siblings held its lock longer than the redelivery budget could outlast, so the fix is capacity or lock granularity, not the task; workspace_unbound means the task was never eligible to run at all because workspace binding failed, which is a configuration or environment fault of a different kind. A low background rate is acceptable, since user tasks do fail. Rising lock_contention_exhausted says sibling tasks on one session hold locks past the redelivery budget. A spike in workspace_unbound is almost always a bad deploy or bad config and should be pinnable to a specific moment.

panels.title: Poison Deferrals by cause
panels.description: The rate at which the poison guard declines to act — it cannot prove the message is poisoned, so it naks for another round instead of reporting a possibly-live task as failed. The four causes mean different things. already_running: the lock carries this message's own sequence, so a handler really is executing it and waiting is correct. already_running_final: the same situation but on the final delivery, where the message is left unsettled instead (see the adjacent stat panel). unknown_holder: the lock is held but carries no seq field, which only a pod from before that field existed can write — a rolling-upgrade artifact. probe_failed: the lock could not be read at all, which means the KV read is broken, not any task. Read the relative heights and trends rather than absolute values; these are conservative waits, not errors. A steady baseline of already_running is normal. unknown_holder should only appear inside an upgrade window and must fall back to zero once the old pods are gone — if it does not, a pre-seq brain instance is still in the cluster. Any sustained probe_failed points at NATS KV read failures, so look at NATS-side metrics rather than at individual tasks.

panels.title: INV-13 Lock Release Skips by reason
panels.description: The rate at which the INV-13 protection fires, split by the three ways release detects it must not delete the lock (these are the only three call sites in tasks/lock.ts). not_holder: the holderId read back from KV is no longer this pod's, so the lock was taken over — typically because this pod's event loop stalled past the lock bucket's TTL. cas_lost: the conditional delete was rejected because the KV revision moved between the get() and the delete(), meaning a competitor wrote into that window. legacy_format: the lock value is a bare pre-INV-13 string rather than JSON, so the holder cannot be identified safely and the entry is neither claimed nor deleted — it is left for the bucket TTL to reap. Read the three lines as three strengths of evidence about who is competing for the lock: not_holder and cas_lost are real concurrent contention, legacy_format is only version residue. In steady state all three should sit at zero. Rising not_holder or cas_lost means a pod is stalling or multiple replicas are contending for one session — check it against claw_brain_watchdog_last_tick_age_seconds. legacy_format should appear only during an upgrade window; if it persists after every old pod is gone, an un-upgraded brain instance is still running.

panels.title: Poison Outcome Breakdown (24h)
panels.description: Puts the poison guard's two possible endings side by side, aligned on the same reason label: discarded is "declared dead and closed out successfully", unresolved is "declared dead but the closing path itself kept failing, so the message was terminated with the session still marked running". Both use the same TerminalRefusalReason domain (max_retries_exceeded / lock_contention_exhausted / workspace_unbound), so one row reads as two fates of the same class of task. Read it as a 24h roster: for each reason, how many tasks were written off cleanly and how many were abandoned outright. Numbers in the discarded column are normal — tasks do fail — and what matters there is whether the mix shifts suddenly. The unresolved column must be empty or all zeros: every increment is a stuck session that needs manual closure, and it indicts the terminal handoff (event emitter, pending-callback outbox, task callback) rather than the task. When unresolved is non-zero, look at which reason it lands on: all three at once suggests the handoff path is broken as a whole, while a single reason points at that one path. This table is also the worklist when stuck sessions have to be closed by hand.

panels.title: Mean Snapshot Size
panels.description: The average size of a session's persisted workspace snapshot, taken from the `size_bytes` field of the meta.json that the sync script writes after each successful copy, aggregated over every brain pod as the ratio of claw_brain_workspace_sync_bytes_sum to _count. This histogram carries no `kind` label, so normal turn-driven syncs and SIGTERM rescue syncs are pooled into the same average. Read it as "how large is a typical /workspace right now": it is the direct input to rsync wall time, so when this climbs the sync duration quantiles below climb with it. Sessions doing ordinary source-and-artifact work usually sit in the single-megabyte to low-hundreds-of-megabytes range; an average in the gigabytes means sessions are writing large rebuildable or bulk artifacts (model weights, build caches, long logs) into /workspace, and past a few gigabytes a single rsync starts to risk the HANDS_CALL_RSYNC_TIMEOUT_MS budget (default 300s) and turns into reason="timeout" in the failure table. Bear in mind a mean is easily dragged up by one outsized session, so confirm against the duration distribution heatmap before concluding the whole fleet grew — and note the sync script already excludes rebuildable caches (.git, node_modules, .cache, __pycache__, torchinductor_*, hsa, worktree, *.co, *.o), so growth here is real payload, not compiler scratch.

panels.title: Worst-Pod Semaphore Slots
panels.description: The most-loaded single brain pod's occupancy of the workspace-sync semaphores. These semaphores are per-process, not cluster-wide, so the fleet-summed panel below can look idle while one pod is individually saturated; `max by (kind)` picks the worst pod so the reading can be compared against the real per-pod ceiling, which is WORKSPACE_SYNC_NORMAL_SLOTS for kind="normal" and WORKSPACE_SIGTERM_PRIORITY_SLOTS for kind="sigterm" (both default 4). The inflight needle at the ceiling means that pod has no free sync slot, and the queued reading is then the backlog parked behind it. Two or fewer inflight is comfortable; three is the warning band; sitting at 4 with queued above zero means end-of-turn persistence on that pod is being serialised, and a rolling restart arriving in that state is unlikely to drain the normal queue before the pods go away. Distinguish skew (one pod pinned, the rest empty — investigate session placement) from genuine shortage (the summed panel is also at its ceiling), because only the second is a reason to raise WORKSPACE_SYNC_NORMAL_SLOTS. The gauge maximum assumes the default of 4 slots per pod; raise it if you changed either slot setting.

panels.title: Sync Rate — Success vs Failure
panels.description: How often workspace syncs happen, split by outcome and by path. The `kind` label has exactly two values: "normal", the routine sync driven by turn completion, and "sigterm", the priority rescue sync taken when the brain process is being terminated. Successes come from the rate of the duration histogram's _count, failures from the rate of claw_brain_workspace_sync_failures_total; both are events per second, so they share one axis. The normal series tracks session activity, while the sigterm series should hug zero and only spike during a rolling deploy, a pod eviction, or a node being reclaimed underneath a sandbox. The failure series is the one to watch. It should stay flat at zero: failures rising together with a sigterm spike mean the rescue sync did not finish inside the termination window and those sessions lose their workspace; failures persisting with no sigterm traffic at all mean the routine path itself is broken, and the reason table says which of the six classifications applies. The inverse signal matters too — if success drops to zero while tasks are clearly still running, syncs are usually blocked on the semaphore (see the saturation panel) rather than absent for lack of demand.

panels.title: Sync Duration Quantiles
panels.description: End-to-end wall time of one syncWorkspace() RPC as measured brain-side — including the wait for the sandbox-side rsync and the meta.json read-back — as p50/p95/p99 split by kind="normal" and kind="sigterm". Use p50 for the steady state and p95/p99 for the tail. The sigterm line is the consequential one: the rescue sync runs inside a bounded termination window (the upstream chart sets terminationGracePeriodSeconds=300 and the SIGTERM budget reserves roughly 60s of it for the priority workspace sync), and a rescue sync that does not finish is a lost workspace. Read the top of the chart with care: the histogram's buckets stop at 120s (0.1/0.5/1/5/10/30/60/120) while the rsync call itself is allowed 300s by HANDS_CALL_RSYNC_TIMEOUT_MS, so every sample above 120s lands in +Inf and histogram_quantile can only report the 120s lower bound — the line flattens against 120 and is not a true value there. Expect p50 under a second and p95 in the single-digit seconds; p95 crossing 30s means snapshots grew or the shared filesystem slowed down; p99 pinned at 120s means samples are already walking toward the 300s ceiling and reason="timeout" will start appearing in the failure table shortly after.

panels.title: Sync Duration Distribution
panels.description: The full shape of the same duration histogram, with normal and sigterm merged, over the bucket edges 0.1/0.5/1/5/10/30/60/120 seconds. The quantile panel above reduces this to three lines; this one keeps the whole distribution. Time runs along the x axis, duration bucket up the y axis, and colour intensity is the rate of samples landing in that bucket. A healthy fleet shows a single dark band pinned to the bottom rows, under a second. The pattern worth catching is bimodality — the normal band at the bottom plus a second band up in the 30s-120s rows — which says a subset of sessions has grown a workspace that rsync struggles with, while the rest are fine; that split is invisible in both the mean and p50 and only shows up here. The +Inf row lighting up is the leading indicator for hitting the 300s rsync timeout, since anything past the 120s top bucket is already more than a third of the way to it.

panels.title: Sync Failures by Reason
panels.description: Workspace sync failures over the last hour, broken out by `kind` ("normal" or "sigterm", the path that failed) and by `reason`, which classifySyncFailure() derives from the thrown error and which has six values: "timeout" (the hands call exceeded HANDS_CALL_RSYNC_TIMEOUT_MS, 300s by default), "hands_unreachable" (the sandbox's hands endpoint could not be reached — usually the pod is already gone or the network broke), "meta_write_error" (meta.json was written but could not be parsed back), "config_error" (workspace_persist_base_missing — the shared persistence root is not mounted), "empty_workspace" (the script refused to overwrite a non-empty snapshot with an empty source directory), and "rsync_error", the catch-all for a script that did not end with its OK marker. Read it as a ranked list: find the dominant reason first, then investigate that. An empty table is the normal state. Mostly timeout points at snapshot size and the duration panels — the data grew. Mostly hands_unreachable is a sandbox-side event, typically a pod being reclaimed, and not a defect in the sync path. A single config_error deserves immediate attention: it means that pod's persistence root is not mounted and every sync it attempts is a no-op. empty_workspace is the guard doing its job against a half-torn-down sandbox mount, so a run of them means sandboxes are disappearing mid-turn. A high share of rsync_error means the real cause was not classified; go read the `err` field on the workspace_sync.failed log line.

panels.title: Sync Semaphore Saturation
panels.description: Saturation of the workspace-sync concurrency semaphores, summed across brain pods. The two gauges are two halves of one story: inflight is the number of syncs actually running, queued is the number already parked waiting for a slot, and the semaphore rewrites both on every state change, so they are always consistent with each other without any polling. There are two independent semaphores: kind="normal" bounded by WORKSPACE_SYNC_NORMAL_SLOTS (default 4 per pod) and kind="sigterm" bounded by WORKSPACE_SIGTERM_PRIORITY_SLOTS (default 4 per pod), the latter existing purely so a rolling restart's rescue syncs are never starved behind routine traffic. Because this panel sums over pods, the fleet ceiling per kind is slots x brain replicas — 12 with the upstream defaults of 4 slots and brain.replicas=3 — and the threshold is set from that; recompute it if you changed either the slot count or the replica count. Queued sitting at zero means concurrency is sufficient. Brief queue spikes are harmless; queued persistently above zero while inflight rides the ceiling means sync has become the bottleneck, every turn's wrap-up is waiting on a slot, and part of what the duration panels report as latency is really queue time. The sigterm pair should be flat zero outside deploys — non-zero at any other time means pods are being terminated or reclaimed.

panels.title: Turns With Zero Breakpoints
panels.description: The share of LLM turns that went out carrying no cache_control marker at all, taken as the lowest histogram bucket (le="0") of claw_brain_llm_cache_breakpoints_sent divided by its total observation count. It lifts the most dangerous row of the breakpoint heatmap out into a single number you can alert on: a turn with no marker cannot hit the cache, so it is billed as a full-price prompt no matter how well the rest of the fleet is doing. Read it as a fraction of turns, not of tokens — one unmarked turn on a very long conversation costs far more than the ratio suggests. Normal is 0 or within rounding of it. Above a few percent, look for the three usual causes: a session that latched its cache off after the gateway rejected a marker (cross-check claw_brain_llm_cache_disabled_total), messages with nothing legally markable in them (a run of thinking blocks, an assistant turn that is only tool calls), or PROMPT_CACHE_ENABLED turned off — that flag is read once at import, so it changes only on a rolling restart. A value near 1 means caching is effectively off fleet-wide.

panels.title: LLM Token Flow by Kind
panels.description: Token rate in tokens/second split by how the tokens were billed, summed over every brain replica. The kind label has exactly four values: input (the prompt that missed cache and was charged in full), output, cache_read (the cheap, cached part of the prompt) and cache_create (writing a new entry, priced slightly above input). The semantics of an absent line are load-bearing: a kind with no series means this provider path cannot report that number, which is not the same as zero — the OpenAI-shaped path never assigns cache_create, and drawing that structural gap as a flat zero is precisely the failure this metric group was built to catch, so never fill it in mentally. Healthy shape: cache_read is the tallest line by roughly an order of magnitude over input, because each turn re-reads a long prefix and adds only a little new text. Worry when input stays at or above cache_read for a sustained period — every turn is recomputing the prefix — or when cache_create tracks cache_read at comparable magnitude, which means entries are being written and then immediately rewritten each turn: you pay the write premium and never collect the read discount.

panels.title: Cache Turns by State
panels.description: Rate of LLM turns classified by what the prompt cache actually did, with the state chosen by a strict priority ladder in metrics.ts: hit (cache_read > 0), write (no read but cache_create > 0), miss (the response explicitly reported the cache fields and they were zero, i.e. a real miss), unreported (caching was enabled but the provider said nothing about it, so this turn could not be measured and must never be counted as a miss), and off (we sent no marker and nothing came back). The distinction between miss and unreported is the point of the metric: both cache counters default to zero, so a turn whose usage chunk never arrived produces the exact digits of a genuine miss, and counting it as one moves a hit-rate denominator on a measurement that was never taken. Stack the series to read composition. Normal is hit dominating, with write appearing as small clusters at session start and just after a compaction. Sustained unreported means that route never returns usage and any hit-rate figure derived from it is not trustworthy; miss rising together with write means the prefix is being broken and rebuilt repeatedly; a jump in off should be checked against claw_brain_llm_cache_disabled_total, since a session latches markers off for good once the gateway rejects one.

panels.title: Breakpoints Sent per Request
panels.description: Distribution of how many cache_control markers each request actually carried, bucketed at [0,1,2,3,4] — four is Anthropic's hard per-request limit (MAX_BREAKPOINTS), spent as one anchor plus up to three rolling markers (ROLLING_TARGET). The count is taken off the request body that was sent, not off the plan that was computed, which is the only way to see a planner/renderer disagreement or a marker silently dropped on the way out. Colour should sit almost entirely on the top rows. Normal is the bulk of requests at 3 or 4. Mass at 0 means no markers are going out at all and caching is effectively disabled for those turns — check claw_brain_llm_cache_disabled_total and PROMPT_CACHE_ENABLED. Mass at 1–2 means the rolling markers are not advancing, usually a markability problem (a message ending in thinking blocks, roles that cannot carry a marker on the OpenAI-shaped path); the consequence is that consecutive markers drift past the API's 20-content-block backward lookup window, the chain stops linking, and the prefix is silently rewritten. The signature failure to watch for is markers going out on this panel while the cache_read rate stays at zero — read this panel side by side with the hit-rate panels, because neither half states the problem alone.

panels.title: Cache Entry Lost by Gap
panels.description: Hourly count of cache entries that were written and then did not survive to the next turn, split by how long the gap between two cache uses was. This is the behavioural complement to the granted-TTL label and the more trustworthy half of the pair: it ignores what the gateway claims it wrote and looks only at what happened — this turn sent markers, the same run had used the cache earlier, the response explicitly reported cache_read, and that read was zero. Because it depends on nothing the usage object chooses to volunteer, it works on transports that report no TTL breakdown at all. The gap is measured from the last turn that touched the cache at all — read or write — and anchored at request time, so a session that keeps hitting keeps its entry alive. That timestamp is checkpointed, so a run resumed on another pod after a redelivery still knows an entry existed and still counts the loss. gap="over_ttl" means the entry vanished across a gap at least as long as the configured LLM_CACHE_TTL, consistent with an entry shorter-lived than the one requested — go to the write-tokens-by-TTL panel next. gap="under_ttl" points at the prefix rather than the lifetime: the tool list changed, the backend switched, or the entry was evicted. Normal is both series flat at zero. Any non-zero value deserves an attribution; sustained over_ttl means long-sleeping sessions are recomputing their whole prefix at full price on every wake-up, which is exactly what paying the 1h write premium was supposed to prevent.

panels.title: Cache Write Tokens by Granted TTL
panels.description: Rate of cache-write tokens split by the lifetime the gateway actually granted, with ttl taking the values "1h", "5m" and "unreported". LLM_CACHE_TTL defaults to 1h, so unless an operator changed it every marker we send asks for 1h; compare this panel against whatever your deployment sets. The panel exists because a gateway that quietly answers a 1h marker with a 5m entry is a 200 OK failure — the request succeeds, the cache genuinely works, and the entry expires under exactly the sleep it was chosen to outlast — and no other number here shows it. "unreported" means the gateway sent no lifetime breakdown (an OpenAI-shaped streaming response gives none); it is not a zero and must not be read as one. Normal is essentially all 1h. A visible 5m curve means the gateway is downgrading the request, and you should see claw_brain_llm_cache_entry_lost_total{gap="over_ttl"} rise alongside it. If unreported dominates, TTL simply cannot be verified on that route and you have to fall back on the behavioural entry-lost counter.

panels.title: Cache Write TTL Share (24h)
panels.description: How many cache-write tokens landed under each granted lifetime over the last 24 hours, read as a ranked name-and-number bar: did today's spend buy 1h entries or 5m entries? It is the same counter as the rate panel above, read for daily composition instead of trend — that one catches the moment of a change, this one tells you how much of the day was affected. Normal is 1h holding the overwhelming majority with 5m at or near zero. Worry when 5m is comparable to 1h: the gateway is systematically downgrading TTL requests, and every session that sleeps longer than five minutes between turns will find its cache gone. A large unreported bar means the day's dominant route sends no lifetime breakdown, so the TTL dimension is unusable for that period and the entry-lost counter is your only evidence.

panels.title: Auto-Compaction Outcomes
panels.description: Hourly count of auto-compaction runs — the pass that summarises older messages so a conversation stays inside the context window — split by the three results compactConversation returns: compacted (messages were actually replaced by a summary), noop (nothing was eligible), failed (summary generation failed and the run continued on the original messages). It only fires on the top-level loop (depth 0) and only when the turn's prompt exceeds COMPACTION_TRIGGER_INPUT_TOKENS, which defaults to 850000 tokens; if your deployment lowers that, expect proportionally more events. Counts are naturally sparse, which is why this is a 1h increase rather than an instantaneous rate. It is tightly coupled to the cache: a successful compaction rewrites the prefix, so the turn immediately after it cannot read cache (the loop clears its last-cache-use timestamp at that point precisely so this does not show up as a lost entry), and a dip in hit rate lined up with a compacted spike is expected rather than a fault. Normal is sparse compacted/noop with failed flat at zero. Repeated failed means the only guard against context growth is not working and the session will eventually be rejected by the context window; a sudden rise in compacted frequency means prompts are growing abnormally fast.

panels.title: Cumulative Tokens Since Restart
panels.description: Total tokens accumulated by kind since each brain process started, laid out as a name-and-number table. This is the one place in this row where a raw counter sum rather than a rate is the right reading, because the question is cumulative: how much has been spent so far and how much of it was served from cache. Treat it as process-scoped — any brain pod restart zeroes that pod's contribution, so the numbers only mean anything in the context of "since the last rolling deploy" and are not a billing record. Normal is cache_read far exceeding input, typically by orders of magnitude, since each turn re-reads a long prefix and contributes only a short tail as fresh input. The row to react to is a missing or zero cache_read alongside a large cache_create: that is a cache being written and never read, the static snapshot of a prefix that is invalidated between every turn, and it can run for a long time without any request failing.

panels.title: Download failure ratio
