panels.description: The share of GET /internal/assets/hands-binary requests over the last 15 minutes that ended in something other than ok — that is, unauthorized, forbidden or not_available taken together. The denominator is wrapped in clamp_min so an idle window with no requests reads 0 rather than NaN; a flat 0 therefore means either no failures or no traffic, and the by-outcome timeseries below is what tells the two apart. Zero is the expected value: none of the three failure outcomes is transient network noise. unauthorized and forbidden are token problems and not_available is a packaging problem, so any sustained non-zero reading points at a specific misconfiguration rather than at load. Treat a few tenths of a percent as a prompt to check which outcome is firing; a couple of percent means a meaningful slice of sandbox cold starts cannot fetch the binary, which surfaces downstream as sandbox_health_failed once the Hands readiness poll (HANDS_HEALTH_MAX_TRIES x HANDS_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS, 40 x 3s by default) runs out. One blind spot to keep in mind: the route only counts a download on the stream's end event, and its error handler is a no-op, so a transfer aborted mid-stream is counted neither as ok nor as a failure. The true failure rate can only be higher than what this gauge shows, never lower.

panels.title: Successful downloads (cumulative)
panels.description: The raw counter sum of hands-binary transfers that streamed to completion, across all Brain pods, since each pod's process started — no rate, no window. Read it as a since-last-restart total: a rolling update resets every pod's counter, so the step down you see after a deploy is the restart, not a fault. What is worth watching is the slope. It should climb steadily in step with sandbox cold starts, because bootstrap tries three sources in ascending cost (in_image, then shared_storage when CLAW_DEPLOY_ROOT is set, then brain_http when BRAIN_HTTP_URL is set) and only reaches this endpoint when the first two are absent or unusable. A flat line while sandboxes are being created is therefore ambiguous in a useful way: either the deployment bakes the binary into its images or mounts it on shared storage and never needs the HTTP fallback — the cheap and desirable case — or brain_http was never registered as a source at all because BRAIN_HTTP_URL is empty, in which case sandboxes on images without their own binary have no third source to fall back to and simply fail to start Hands.

panels.title: Average bytes per download
panels.description: Mean size of one successful transfer, computed as the byte rate divided by the ok request rate over a 30-minute window. This is an integrity check, not a capacity figure: the served file is a single fixed artifact, so the average should sit flat at whatever the current Hands binary weighs (on the order of 90MB, drifting slowly as the binary is rebuilt) and change only in a clean step when a new version ships. Both numerator and denominator are rates, so idle periods read 0. An average that settles well below the binary's real size is the signal to act on. Because bytes are accumulated per chunk while the ok count is incremented only on the stream's end event, a value that is short means end fired on a transfer that did not actually deliver the whole file — typically the sandbox side closing the connection early. Correlate with the sandbox-side bootstrap errors, which reject exactly this case with "hands-binary is empty after download" or "hands-binary download failed" before Hands is ever launched. A sudden clean jump in either direction, with no shortfall afterwards, is just a new binary.

panels.title: Hands binary download rate by outcome
panels.description: Request rate on GET /internal/assets/hands-binary split by outcome, which is the metric's only label and a closed set of four: ok, unauthorized, forbidden, not_available. Sandbox bootstrap reaches this endpoint only as its last resort, after the in-image path and the shared-storage mount have been tried, so on a deployment whose tenant images do not ship /app/hands-binary and do not mount CLAW_DEPLOY_ROOT this curve is effectively the sandbox cold-start rate — a real load signal rather than a corner-case counter. Counters from every Brain pod are summed here, so read it as cluster-wide throughput; ok rising and falling with bursts of session creation is normal. The other three lines should be flat at zero. unauthorized (401, no Bearer header at all) and forbidden (403, token present but not found) persisting means hands-token issuance is broken, or the cross-pod lookup that resolves a token from the NATS KV bucket is failing or timing out, so a sandbox authenticating against a pod other than the one that minted its token gets turned away. not_available (503) means the pod serving the request has no file at BRAIN_BUNDLED_HANDS_BINARY (default /app/hands-binary): every sandbox that load-balances onto that pod loses its last source, so even a single occurrence is a packaging defect in that image worth chasing immediately.

panels.title: Hands binary egress bandwidth
panels.description: Bytes per second actually leaving this endpoint. The underlying counter carries no labels and is advanced only on successful transfers, chunk by chunk as they stream. It matters because the HTTP fallback is the expensive source by design: each sandbox that reaches it pulls the whole binary — roughly 90MB — from whichever Brain pod the Service picks, so a burst of concurrent cold starts turns into gigabytes of egress competing with Brain's own LLM and NATS traffic for the same NIC and memory bandwidth. All pods are summed, so this is cluster-wide egress; its shape should track the ok line on the by-outcome panel, since it is the same events measured in bytes. Spikes synchronised with cold-start waves and a near-zero floor between them are normal. A line that sits pinned near the link's ceiling for long stretches means a cold-start storm is amplifying itself, and the fix is not more Brain replicas: bake the binary into the tenant image at /app/hands-binary, or mount CLAW_DEPLOY_ROOT, so bootstrap stops at one of the first two sources and never pays for the transfer.

panels.title: Download duration p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Quantiles and mean of the time spent streaming the binary on successful downloads, the trend view of the same histogram shown as a heatmap, easy to line up against releases and scaling events. p50 is what a typical cold start waits for its binary; p95 and p99 are the slowest sandboxes in the wave. The mean comes from _sum over _count, so a mean sitting above p95 is meaningful: the histogram's top explicit bucket is 60s, quantiles are clamped at that boundary, and the mean is not — transfers landing in +Inf show up only there. What counts as slow follows from the bootstrap budget rather than from taste. The start_hands step is bounded by HANDS_BOOTSTRAP_START_TIMEOUT (150s by default) and covers download, launch and the env-file wait, while readiness afterwards gets HANDS_HEALTH_MAX_TRIES x HANDS_HEALTH_INTERVAL_MS (40 x 3s = 120s). A p50 of a few seconds and a p95 in the single digits leave that budget comfortable. p95 climbing past ten seconds says concurrent cold starts are already contending for bandwidth; p99 pressed up against the 30s and 60s buckets means the transfer alone is consuming most of the start budget, and the next thing to appear will be sandboxes failing readiness in batches. Raise the expectations here if you have changed either timeout.

panels.title: Downloads by brain pod
panels.description: Successful hands-binary transfers served by each individual Brain pod over the past hour — the one panel in this row that deliberately does not aggregate across pods, because balance is the whole question. Sandboxes reach Brain through the ClusterIP Service, so with the chart's default of three Brain replicas the bars should be roughly level; a spread within about a factor of two is unremarkable given that cold starts arrive in bursts. One pod standing well above the rest means it is carrying the egress for cold starts largely on its own, and its network and GC pressure will degrade before its peers' do — check for a stale or sticky client-side endpoint list. A pod sitting at zero while the others work is the case to act on, especially alongside not_available on the by-outcome panel: that pod's image is missing the file at BRAIN_BUNDLED_HANDS_BINARY (default /app/hands-binary), and every sandbox the Service routes to it gets a 503 instead of a binary. Scale the expected bar heights to your own replica count.

panels.title: Destructive rebuild share of recoveries
panels.description: The fraction of all in-flight recovery decisions that came back as decision="rebuilt" — that is, how often repairing a session required destroying the sandbox and putting a replacement in its place. This is the one number in this row that directly quantifies running user work being thrown away: a rebuild restores /workspace from the last checkpoint, but every background shell started with bash(run_in_background), every long-running job and every GPU workload inside the old container is gone, and the model is told explicitly to redo them. The two non-destructive outcomes, reconnected and hands_restarted, keep all of it. Read it as a ratio of fleet-wide rates and watch the trend rather than any single point; when recovery traffic is light the denominator is tiny and the reading jumps, so confirm against the decision-rate panel that there were meaningful attempts at all. Below roughly 20% is healthy — most sandbox faults should be fixable by restarting Hands in place or by rebuilding Brain's MCP client. A sustained 20–50% means the data-plane probe is returning dead often, which usually tracks node preemption or the control plane removing workloads underneath running sessions. Above 50%, check whether SANDBOX_HANDS_RESTART_ENABLED (default true) has been turned off: with it off, every session that could have been repaired in place degrades into a rebuild, this ratio rises across the board, and the only symptom users see is background jobs disappearing for no stated reason. Note also that rebuilds are budgeted per task (SANDBOX_REBUILD_MAX_PER_TASK, default 3), so a high ratio also burns that budget quickly.

panels.title: Unrepaired recovery share (left_alone / failed / exhausted)
panels.description: The share of recovery attempts after which the session was no better off than before. Three decisions are folded together because they are indistinguishable from the user's side: left_alone means nothing could be established so nothing was touched, failed means the recovery attempt itself threw (the clearest case being a DAG node refusing to destroy a sandbox it inherited), and exhausted means the per-task rebuild or recovery budget refused the attempt (SANDBOX_REBUILD_MAX_PER_TASK and SANDBOX_RECOVERY_MAX_PER_TASK, both default 3) or the recovery was refused outright. That refusal is latched: once it fires, the loop stops re-probing for the rest of the task rather than paying for the same answer every batch. In all three cases tool calls keep failing and the model is told to stop retrying and report only what it finished, so one combined ratio is the right view. Under 10% is normal. Between 10% and 30% means a set of tasks is stuck in an unrepairable state. Above 30% the probe side is almost certainly returning unknown at scale — an unreachable control plane or KV bucket — because unknown licenses neither a destroy nor a leave-alone, so recovery can only choose left_alone until the budget runs out and turns into exhausted. When that happens, go to the verdict x reason table in this row and look for kv_unreachable, exec_unreachable and exec_deadline. Adjust the bands if you have raised either per-task budget.

panels.title: Sweeper-evicted stale KV entries
panels.description: claw_sandbox_sweeper_evicted_total counts stale Hands KV entries removed by the background sweeper; it carries no labels, so this is a single global count. Every pass (roughly every five minutes) the sweeper walks the hands.* keys and health-checks each Hands endpoint with an HTTP GET /health on a 3s timeout; only after SANDBOX_SWEEPER_EVICT_AFTER_FAILURES consecutive failures does it actually stop the workload and delete the entry. That threshold defaults to 0, which disables sweeper-driven eviction entirely — health checks still run and log, but nothing is ever stopped — so on a default deployment this counter is expected to stay flat at zero forever, and any movement at all means an operator opted in by setting it above 0. Entries in status=pending are never reaped regardless: they belong to an in-flight sandbox creation that may legitimately be waiting on a slow GPU queue. The green line is the per-second eviction rate; the second series is the rolling one-hour total, which is the easier one for answering "how many did we clean up today". With eviction enabled, occasional single-digit hourly counts are fine and just mean some sessions exited badly and left dirty entries behind. A persistently non-zero rate deserves attention: Hands' health route going dark is not proof the container is dead — a codeinterpreter crash or a stalled filesystem flush produces exactly that while exec still works — and the sweeper's eviction really does kill whatever background work is running inside, so sustained eviction is loss as much as cleanup.

panels.title: Incomplete session cleanup by reason
panels.description: Counts session teardowns that could not confirm they had removed everything they owned and therefore handed the session to the idle-reclaim path instead. The reason label domain is derived from SessionDestroyResult — no_platform_key, lookup_failed, delete_failed, list_truncated — plus two the caller alone can produce: threw for an exception on the way through, and unknown for an incomplete result that named no reason. Read it as fleet-wide rate split by reason, because the reasons point at completely different faults: lookup_failed and list_truncated are enumeration problems on the platform side, meaning some workloads were never listed and so never considered for deletion; delete_failed means the delete was attempted and rejected; no_platform_key means the session record was missing the key needed to address the workload at all; threw is a code path fault inside Brain itself. Steady state is zero. A reading here is not proof of a leak on its own — the sweeper reclaims clusters on its next pass and the control plane's idle GC eventually takes the pod — but it does mean a delete did not take effect when it was issued, so the resources stay allocated longer than they should. A sustained rate on any reason points at trouble in the sandbox platform rather than at a transient.

panels.title: Sandbox liveness verdict at resume
panels.description: claw_brain_sandbox_probe_total records what Brain concluded about the previous sandbox when a task resumes, including resumes triggered by NATS redelivery; it is recorded once per run, so this is a classification of resume paths rather than a probe rate. The result label has four values: alive (a KV entry exists and the sandbox is up, so /workspace can be reused as is), alive_no_kv (the sandbox was reused but no v3 checkpoint was read back, so the working directory survived and the conversation state did not), dead (ensureHands had to build a sandbox, so /workspace is restored from the last checkpoint if one exists), and no_hands (the run never had a sandbox attached in the first place). The bar gauge ranks cumulative counts over the selected range; pair it with claw_brain_resume_workspace_mode_total, which carries the SLO-1a/SLO-1b resume classification, for the complete picture. dead is recorded whenever ensureHands had to build a sandbox, which includes every new session's first one, so its share tracks new-session volume as much as sandbox loss; read it against claw_brain_resume_workspace_mode_total{mode="skip_no_ckpt"} to separate fresh starts from genuine rebuilds of resumed work. alive_no_kv is the ordinary shape of a new message arriving on a still-warm sandbox, since the checkpoint key is per message and is deleted when a run completes. It only means something is wrong when it rises on runs that were redeliveries — cross-check claw_brain_checkpoint_resume_total{result="miss_redelivery"}, which is the same event counted where the distinction is made.

panels.title: Container data-plane probe verdict rate
panels.description: claw_brain_sandbox_container_probe_total measures liveness by running a trivial command inside the container over the data-plane exec path, deliberately independent of the Hands MCP port. Hands going dark is not the same as the container being gone — a codeinterpreter crash or a stalled filesystem flush drops MCP while exec still succeeds — and treating the former as the latter is how a live workload gets SIGTERMed. The verdict is three-valued rather than boolean: alive means a command really did run in there just now, dead means there is explicit evidence the container is gone or cannot run anything, and unknown means nobody could be reached to ask. Read the three rates together, keeping the asymmetry in mind: only dead licenses a destroy and only alive licenses leaving things alone, so unknown means retry rather than act. alive should dominate. A low background rate of dead is expected wherever nodes get preempted or reclaimed. The line to worry about is unknown trending up: it says the control plane or the KV bucket is unreachable, and while that lasts every in-flight recovery stalls — sessions present as making no progress rather than as failing, which is much harder to notice.

panels.title: Probe verdict x evidence reason
panels.description: The same probe counter broken out by its reason label, because "the probe said no" is not actionable on its own — the reason is what names the thing to fix. Both label domains are closed unions in the probe source, so the combination is bounded at roughly thirty series: reasons are exec_ok, exec_nonzero, exec_no_exit_code, exec_sandbox_gone, exec_unreachable, exec_deadline, kv_unreachable, no_kv_entry, entry_unusable, entry_corrupt and aborted. Read it as a ranked table of verdict+reason totals over the selected range. The characteristic pairings are alive/exec_ok for healthy, dead/no_kv_entry for a session with no addressable identity left, dead/exec_sandbox_gone for the control plane stating outright that it does not exist, unknown/kv_unreachable for a KV bucket that could not be read, unknown/entry_corrupt for bytes in KV that would not parse as JSON, and unknown/exec_deadline for hitting the probe's own 8-second ceiling. Note what no_kv_entry does and does not tell you: the entry was deleted, or its TTL expired over a container that may still be running, so it is the one dead verdict that is not evidence about the container — it is safe only because without a workloadId nothing destructive is possible. Two further things deserve attention. Keep entry_corrupt and no_kv_entry distinct: corrupt yields unknown, which forbids touching the container, so that sandbox can never be repaired and every recovery round spends budget for nothing, whereas an absent entry yields dead and can be rebuilt. And a persistent exec_deadline means the probe is eating tool-batch time while the agent loop waits on it.

panels.title: Container probe duration distribution (8s ceiling)
panels.description: Wall-clock time for a single container probe, including the control-plane call, bucketed at 0.05/0.1/0.25/0.5/1/2/4/8 seconds — a ladder chosen around the probe's own 8-second deadline. The colour is the rate of probes landing in each duration bucket. This probe sits on the critical path of a tool batch: the agent loop is blocked on it while deciding whether to rebuild, so time spent here is dead time the user experiences as a pause, which is why the distribution rather than an average is what matters. The bright band should sit between roughly 0.05s and 0.5s. Mass moving into 1–4s means the control plane is getting slower. Sustained colour in the 8s bucket means a large share of probes are hitting the ceiling and being classified unknown (visible as reason=exec_deadline in the verdict x reason table); the consequence is a tool batch that waits eight seconds and is then not allowed to act on the result. Note that the tail is capped by design — the absence of buckets above 8s is not evidence that nothing is slower than that.

panels.title: In-flight recovery decisions (destructive vs non-destructive)
panels.description: What the recovery logic actually did once the probe answered. The decision label is the HandsRecoveryAction union plus the two outcomes no action describes, six values in total, and the useful split is by whether running work survived. Non-destructive: reconnected, where both the container and Hands answered and only Brain's MCP client was stale, so a fresh client re-runs the handshake and nothing inside the sandbox is disturbed; and hands_restarted, where the container was alive but its Hands server was not, so Hands was started again in place — /workspace is untouched, background processes and GPU work keep running, and only the old shell ids stop being addressable. That path is gated on SANDBOX_HANDS_RESTART_ENABLED (default true); turning it off makes sessions that could be repaired in place fall back to rebuilds. Destructive: rebuilt, where the data plane confirmed the container was dead, the sandbox was replaced and /workspace restored from the last checkpoint, with every background shell, long-running job and GPU workload in the old sandbox lost and the model told to redo them. Not a repair at all: left_alone (nothing could be established, so the attempt was spent for nothing), failed (the attempt threw), and exhausted (the per-task rebuild or recovery budget refused, after which this task stops trying). Read the balance between rebuilt and hands_restarted/reconnected. Rebuilt rising means users are losing in-flight work; left_alone, failed and exhausted rising means sessions are entering the state where tools keep failing and nothing can fix them; everything concentrated in reconnected points at Brain's own MCP transport failing repeatedly, with the sandbox not at fault.

panels.title: Reading this row
panels.description: A static notes panel for this row rather than a query. Read this row verdict-first. claw_brain_sandbox_container_probe_total reports what the data plane could establish about a container by running a command inside it; claw_brain_sandbox_recovery_decision_total reports what recovery then did. Hands' MCP port going dark is not evidence the container is gone, so the probe is three-valued: only dead licenses destroying a sandbox, only alive licenses leaving it alone, and unknown means retry. Several thresholds in this row assume upstream defaults — SANDBOX_HANDS_RESTART_ENABLED=true, SANDBOX_REBUILD_MAX_PER_TASK=3, SANDBOX_RECOVERY_MAX_PER_TASK=3, SANDBOX_SWEEPER_EVICT_AFTER_FAILURES=0 (sweeper eviction disabled) — adjust them if your deployment overrides these.

panels.title: Watchdog Tick Age by Pod
panels.description: Seconds since each brain pod's internal watchdog tick last fired. infra/watchdog.ts runs two independent setInterval(1s) timers: one refreshes the anchor timestamp and zeroes claw_brain_watchdog_last_tick_age_seconds, the other separately publishes (now - lastTick) into the same gauge. The split exists so a spike survives between scrapes — a single timer that both anchored and published would erase its own high-water mark the instant the loop recovered. When the event loop stalls (a long major GC, a wedged session callback, a blocking native call) both timers slip together and the gauge climbs. It is deliberately decoupled from the session-level NATS KV keepAlive, because a keepalive driven by one healthy session can renew happily while the pod as a whole is stuck. Read it one line per pod and never aggregate: summing across replicas (chart default brain.replicas=3) buries a single wedged pod under its healthy siblings, which is exactly the failure this panel exists to expose. Steady state oscillates between 0 and 2s; sustained values above 10s mean real event-loop lag and should be cross-read against the GC, CPU and heap panels below to find the cause; above 60s the pod is effectively hung; 60s is the threshold the metric's own help text names, and the natural place to put an alert rule if your deployment has one. A hang there also stops the INV-13 session-lock renewals (default LOCK_REFRESH_INTERVAL_MS=10000 against a BRAIN_REGISTRY_TTL_MS of 5 minutes), so the pod is on a clock before another pod takes over locks it still believes it holds. Any single line entering that band is an immediate per-pod investigation, not a fleet-level one.

panels.title: Open File Descriptors vs Limit
panels.description: Fraction of the process file-descriptor ulimit currently in use (process_open_fds / process_max_fds, from prom-client's default metrics). This is a saturation ratio with a hard ceiling rather than an open-ended quantity, which is why it is a gauge and not a curve. Descriptor leaks — NATS connections, HTTP sockets or file handles that are never closed — kill the process with EMFILE, and that death looks like an ordinary crash from the outside: heap and RSS stay perfectly normal right up to the moment new connections start failing. The panel takes the worst pod, so a single leaking replica cannot hide behind the others. A healthy deployment sits near zero and stays flat, because the steady-state connection set (NATS, Postgres, the HTTP server) is small and bounded; what matters is the shape over hours, not the instantaneous value. Slow monotonic growth that never falls back after load subsides is the leak signature — pair it with nodejs_active_handles_total to identify which handle class is accumulating. Treat sustained usage above 70% as something to chase down before it becomes an outage, and above 90% as imminent: new inbound connections and outbound dials will start being refused.

panels.title: Event Loop Lag (p50 / p90 / p99)
panels.description: Actual Node event-loop delay quantiles. prom-client samples these through monitorEventLoopDelay and exports them as ready-made p50/p90/p99 gauges, not as a histogram — do not wrap them in histogram_quantile. This is the upstream cause of the watchdog panel above: timers only fire late because synchronous work or a stop-the-world GC is holding the loop, so a rise here precedes a rise in tick age. Each line is the worst pod at that instant (max), which keeps one degraded replica visible; the diagnostic signal is the spread between the quantiles. A flat p50 with spiking p99 means occasional long tasks or major GCs — episodic, and usually benign if brief. A p50 that lifts as a whole means the pod is persistently oversubscribed and every request is paying for it, which is a capacity or blocking-code problem rather than a GC one. Line the panel up in time with Watchdog Tick Age: genuine stalls appear in both simultaneously, and a tick-age climb with no corresponding lag points at the timer thread itself rather than the loop. Single-digit milliseconds at p50 and a p99 under 100ms is healthy; a p99 persistently over 100ms warrants investigation, and any quantile crossing a second corresponds to the regime where tick age breaches its 10s warning line.

panels.title: Heap Used vs Heap Total
panels.description: V8 heap occupancy per pod (nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes) plotted against the heap V8 has actually reserved from the OS (nodejs_heap_size_total_bytes). They are two layers of one saturation story and share a bytes axis, so no second y-axis is needed: used is what the program is holding, total is how much room V8 has decided it needs to hold it. A healthy process draws a sawtooth — allocation climbs, a GC cycle drops it back. The thing to watch is not the peaks but whether the troughs rise from cycle to cycle: monotonically rising troughs mean objects are being retained across collections, which is a leak, and the endgame is used pressing against total while total itself keeps ratcheting upward until the process dies. Reading the trough slope is also how you tell a genuine in-process leak from an external OOMKill: a leak shows the ramp before the restart, an externally imposed kill shows a flat heap that simply ends. Tens of megabytes of steady sawtooth is normal for a brain pod; be concerned when troughs climb for hours without recovering, or when used stays above roughly 85% of total, since V8 at that point is spending itself on collection and the next allocation burst has nowhere to go.

panels.title: RSS Memory by Pod
panels.description: Process resident set size per pod — the number the container memory limit and the kernel OOM killer actually measure. It is always larger than the V8 heap because it also covers Buffers and other external memory, native module allocations and the code segment, and that difference is the diagnostic value of having both panels: heap flat while RSS climbs means the leak is in Buffers or native code, not in JS objects, and no amount of heap-snapshot work will find it. Split by pod so a single bad replica is visible; a line dropping vertically to near zero is a process restart, which the uptime table below will confirm. Sawtooth is fine, a monotonic ramp is not. Expect all replicas to sit on the same plateau, roughly an order of magnitude above the heap figure, and expect that plateau to be stable across a day. Approaching 90% of the container memory limit is the point to act, because past it the kill is involuntary and takes any in-flight run with it. A repeating macro-pattern of climb, drop to zero, climb again is the signature of an OOMKill loop rather than of ordinary restarts, and it will keep recurring until either the leak or the limit is changed.

panels.title: CPU Usage by Pod
panels.description: Rate of CPU seconds consumed per pod, i.e. cores in use (1.0 = one core fully saturated). process_cpu_seconds_total is a cumulative counter and must be wrapped in rate(); summing it raw yields total CPU burned since process start, which is not a load signal. Because Node executes JavaScript on a single thread, a pod pinned at 1.0 means the main thread is fully occupied by synchronous work — and that is precisely the condition that drives event-loop lag and watchdog tick age up at the same moment, so all three panels should spike together. Splitting by pod is what separates broad traffic growth (every replica rises together, roughly in proportion) from one replica trapped in a loop (one line detaches and stays up while the others track demand). Normal operation is well below 1.0, with idle pods near zero. Sustained readings above 0.8 mean the single core is nearly exhausted and loop latency is about to degrade; a line parked at 1.0 that does not fall back when traffic does is a pod stuck in synchronous execution, and the next step is a CPU profile of that specific pod rather than a restart, which would only hide the cause.

panels.title: GC Pause Duration Distribution
panels.description: Distribution of V8 garbage-collection pause durations, from prom-client's nodejs_gc_duration_seconds histogram (bucket edges 0.001 / 0.01 / 0.1 / 1 / 2 / 5 seconds, labelled by kind: major, minor, incremental, weakcb). GC is stop-the-world, so a single long major collection freezes the event loop outright and is the most common benign explanation for a watchdog tick-age climb. What matters here is the shape of the distribution rather than any one quantile, hence a heatmap: time on x, pause length on y, colour intensity as the number of collections landing in that bucket during the window. In a healthy process the heat is pinned to the lowest one or two buckets and stays there. A vertical smear reaching into higher buckets is a single long-GC episode — go to Watchdog Tick Age at the same timestamp and you should find the matching spike. Expect the overwhelming majority of collections at or below 1ms, with majors still in the low-milliseconds range. Heat settling into the 0.1s bucket, or any pauses of a second or more, is the point to worry: pauses that long alone can push tick age past its 10s line, and they normally arrive together with a heap that is close to saturated, so read this panel and Heap Used vs Heap Total as one picture.

panels.title: Process Uptime by Pod
panels.description: How long each brain process has been alive, computed as time() minus process_start_time_seconds (the process's Unix start timestamp). It is rendered as a table because it is a list of names against numbers and the only question being asked is which replica is the youngest — a chart adds nothing to that. Any row markedly shorter than its peers is a pod that has recently restarted; take its pod name back to the RSS and Heap panels to see the memory curve leading up to the restart, which is what distinguishes an OOMKill (RSS ramping into the limit) from a crash (an abrupt end with flat memory) from a normal rolling deploy (every row resetting together). Healthy steady state is all replicas showing similar uptimes that grow linearly in step, since they were brought up by the same rollout. Note that a rolling update legitimately resets every row, and with the chart default terminationGracePeriodSeconds=300 the replicas come up staggered rather than simultaneously, so slightly unequal uptimes right after a deploy are expected. A single row that repeatedly falls back to minutes or hours while the others keep climbing is a restart loop; check that pod's RSS curve and its container exit code before anything else.
